issues.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is proved when the propounder establishes its execution and the testator’s testamentary capacity, and the opposing party does not substantiate alleged fraud, coercion, or suspicious circumstances.
material_facts: The testator’s written statement, filed before his death, expressly stated that he had executed the disputed will.
The will was registered, and its registration endorsement recorded the testator’s acknowledgment of execution and signatures of identifying witnesses.
An attesting witness and the scribe testified about the will’s execution; the evidence also supported that the testator was of sound mind.
The opposing parties produced no evidence of fraud, coercion, undue influence, or lack of testamentary capacity.

The lower courts relied on matters including the exclusion of an alleged adopted son, the distribution of most property to the beneficiaries, and the beneficiaries’ presence, which the Supreme Court found insufficient to invalidate the will.
issues.conclusion: The propounders proved that the will was duly executed and was the testator’s last will; the beneficiaries and the widow were entitled to the properties allotted to them under it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act, a document required by law to be attested must be proved through an attesting witness capable of giving evidence. Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act requires the testator’s signature or mark and attestation by two or more witnesses in the manner stated there. Registration does not dispense with proof of execution and attestation, but Section 114 of the Evidence Act permits a presumption that the Registrar’s recorded particulars were regularly and correctly made. The propounder must establish execution and testamentary capacity; the burden then shifts to the contestant to support allegations such as fraud, coercion, or undue influence, and may shift back to the propounder to dispel substantiated suspicious circumstances. The exclusion of natural heirs or a beneficiary’s mere presence does not, by itself, establish suspicion: Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty and Uma Devi Nambiar v. T.C. Sidhan.

rule.if: will_property_dispute_appeal and testator_admitted_execution and attesting_witness_and_scribe_supported_execution and testator_was_of_sound_mind and opposing_party_produced_no_evidence_of_fraud_or_coercion

predicates.will_property_dispute_appeal: An appeal in a property dispute challenged a will offered to determine the parties’ property rights.
predicates.testator_admitted_execution: The person who made the will stated before death that they had executed it.
predicates.attesting_witness_and_scribe_supported_e: An attesting witness and the person who prepared the will gave evidence supporting its execution.
predicates.testator_was_of_sound_mind: The evidence showed that the person who made the will was of sound mind when it was executed.
predicates.opposing_party_produced_no_evidence_of_f: The party opposing the will produced no evidence that it resulted from fraud, coercion, or undue influence.

issues.definition: When a will is disputed in a property appeal, the testator admitted execution, an attesting witness and scribe supported execution, the testator was of sound mind, and the opposing party produced no evidence of fraud or coercion, the will is proved.

issues.legal_issue: An alleged adoption relied on to displace the natural course of succession is not established where the evidence lacks reliable particulars and is contradicted by the alleged adoptive father’s denial and other evidence identifying the claimant as a natural relative.
material_facts: A claimant sought a share of family property on the basis that he had been adopted by the deceased and his wife.
The alleged adoptive father denied the adoption in a written statement filed while he was alive and described the claimant as his brother’s son whom he had looked after.
The pleadings and testimony did not provide a definite date or place for the adoption ceremony, and the witnesses gave only general, similar accounts of the ceremony.
The claimant’s mother did not claim maintenance for him when she raised a maintenance dispute, and the claimant testified that the deceased had neglected him and failed to support his studies.

In other proceedings and records, the claimant was described as the deceased’s brother’s son, and the deceased was described as his guardian; the school forms used a combined ‘father or guardian’ designation.
The evidence relied on to prove the adoption did not, in the Supreme Court’s view, meet the required standard.
issues.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not proved. The claimant acquired no right or interest in the suit properties or mesne profits on the basis of that alleged adoption; the appellants were entitled to the property under the will and could claim mesne profits from the respondents.
issues.legal_principle: A person asserting adoption to divert the ordinary course of succession bears a heavy burden to establish it with reliable and convincing evidence and to explain suspicious circumstances. Oral evidence without a registered adoption document or other clinching evidence must be scrutinised particularly carefully where suspicious circumstances exist. The Court applied Rahasa Pandiani v. Gokulananda Panda and Kishori Lal v. Mt. Chaltibai.

rule.if: property_partition_proceeding and adoption_claim_displaces_natural_succession and alleged_adoptive_parent_denied_adoption and adoption_evidence_lacked_reliable_particulars and contemporaneous_evidence_identified_claimant_as_natural_relative_or_guarded_person

predicates.property_partition_proceeding: A party sought a share of property in a partition or related property proceeding.
predicates.adoption_claim_displaces_natural_success: A party relied on an alleged adoption to obtain property in place of those who would take by the ordinary course of succession.
predicates.alleged_adoptive_parent_denied_adoption: The person said to have adopted the claimant denied the adoption.
predicates.adoption_evidence_lacked_reliable_partic: The evidence supporting the adoption did not reliably establish details of the alleged ceremony or otherwise provide convincing proof.
predicates.contemporaneous_evidence_identified_clai: Other proceedings or records identified the claimant as a natural relative or as someone for whom the alleged adoptive parent acted as guardian.

issues.definition: In a property partition proceeding, an adoption claim that displaces natural succession is not proved when the alleged adoptive parent denied it, the supporting evidence lacked reliable particulars, and other evidence identified the claimant as a natural relative or a person under guardianship.

issues.legal_issue: A spouse who receives property under a will is not entitled to maintenance from the estate on the basis advanced under the provision governing maintenance of dependants.
material_facts: The widow claimed maintenance against the deceased’s estate.
The will allotted property to the widow for her benefit, and the Court held that she was entitled to the property allotted to her.
issues.conclusion: Because the widow was given property under the will, she was not entitled to maintenance under Section 22 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 22 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and held, on the facts, that the widow’s entitlement to property allotted to her under the will precluded the maintenance claim asserted against the estate.

predicates.maintenance_claim_against_estate: A claimant sought maintenance from the estate of a deceased person.
predicates.claimant_received_property_under_will: The claimant received property under the deceased person’s will.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks maintenance from an estate and has received property under the deceased person’s will, the maintenance claim is denied.
